questions.title: How do you run Kanban effectively for a team of six to ten engineers?
questions.quick: I make the work visible with a board whose columns match our real workflow, and I set WIP limits so the team finishes before starting. Each column has explicit policies for what pulling in means. I track cycle time, throughput, work item age, cumulative flow and blocked items, hold a regular replenishment meeting, and use classes of service such as expedite or fixed date so urgent work has a defined, limited lane.
questions.revision: Visible workflow, WIP limits, explicit policies, flow metrics, regular replenishment and classes of service; improve by reading the data.
questions.detailed:
Kanban is a method for managing flow, not just a board. With six to ten engineers the aim is steady delivery and early signals of trouble.

## Board design

Columns mirror how work really moves, for example Ready, In progress, Review, Test, Done, with a waiting sub-column where hand-offs happen. Each column carries a written **policy**: entry and exit criteria, who may pull, what "ready for review" means.

{{diagram:board}}

## WIP limits

Set limits per column or per person-pair, starting near team size and tightening as bottlenecks appear. When a limit is reached, the team swarms on finishing or unblocking, not on starting. Limits expose queues that were previously hidden.

## Flow metrics

| Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Cycle time | How long items take from start to done; use percentiles, not averages |
| Throughput | Items finished per week, used for forecasting |
| Work item age | Which in-flight items are ageing beyond normal cycle time |
| Cumulative flow | Widening bands reveal growing queues |
| Blocked items | Count and duration of blockers, with a named owner for each |

## Cadences

- **Daily stand-up** walks the board right to left, oldest and blocked items first.
- **Replenishment** weekly: agree what enters Ready, based on throughput and priorities.
- **Flow review and retrospective:** inspect the metrics and adjust limits and policies.

## Classes of service

Define a few: **expedite** (strict cap, for genuine emergencies), **fixed date**, **standard** and **intangible** (such as technical debt). Each has an agreed policy so urgency does not silently destroy flow.

## Common mistakes

- No WIP limits, so the board is a to-do list.
- Everything marked expedite.
- Tracking velocity-style numbers and ignoring ageing items.
- Hiding blockers instead of escalating them.
followUps: How do you choose the initial WIP limit?
How do you forecast delivery dates from throughput?
What would you do if the review column is always full?

diagrams.title: Kanban board flow
diagrams.alt: Work moves from a backlog through a replenishment meeting into Ready, In progress, Review, Test and Done, with WIP limits on the active columns. Blocked items are flagged and escalated, and flow metrics from the board feed a regular flow review.

questions.title: How do you lead six to ten engineers while staying hands-on?
questions.quick: I accept that my capacity for critical-path coding shrinks, so I stay technical where it adds most: design, code review, spikes and pairing, not owning the longest task. I reserve time for the team, such as one-to-ones and unblocking, and protect a few focused hours for my own work. I delegate with clear outcomes and let others grow, and use review to coach and maintain standards rather than to rewrite.
questions.revision: Stay technical through design, review and spikes, not critical-path tasks; protect time for people, delegate outcomes, and use review to coach.
questions.detailed:
With six to ten engineers, the technical lead's output is mainly the team's output. Staying close to the code keeps judgement sharp, but it must not make you the bottleneck.

## Time allocation

| Activity | Rough share | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| People and unblocking | 30 to 40% | One-to-ones, questions, hiring, feedback |
| Design and review | 25 to 30% | Architecture, pull request review, ADRs |
| Planning and stakeholders | 15 to 20% | Priorities, risks, communication |
| Own technical work | 10 to 20% | Spikes, tooling, off the critical path |

The figures are a guide; adjust per phase of the project.

{{diagram:time}}

## What to code and what to delegate

- Take spikes, prototypes, internal tooling and test infrastructure. Avoid features with tight deadlines that you cannot guarantee time for.
- Delegate **outcomes**, not step lists: state the goal, constraints and review points, then let the owner choose how.
- Use stretch assignments with support, and pair on the hardest parts.

## Code review role

Review for design, risk and learning. Spread review across senior engineers, set conventions through automation (linting, templates) so reviews focus on substance, and keep turnaround short because slow reviews damage flow.

## Staying credible

Read the code, join incident reviews, pair occasionally and try the tools the team uses. Credibility comes from understanding, not from typing the most lines.

## Common mistakes

- Taking the hardest ticket and then being unavailable.
- Rewriting others' code in review instead of coaching.
- Becoming a single point of knowledge.
- Dropping one-to-ones when busy.
followUps: How do you decide what to delegate and what to keep?
What do you do if your own task is slipping?
How do you keep a good senior engineer growing without making them lead?

diagrams.title: Where a lead spends time
diagrams.alt: A technical lead divides time between people and unblocking, design and review, planning with stakeholders, and own technical work. Delegation and review feed back to the team, increasing capacity and reducing bottlenecks.

questions.title: How do you resolve a long-standing blocker that crosses several teams?
questions.quick: First I find out why it has lasted: unclear ownership, competing priorities or a genuine technical problem. I put the facts on one page with the cost of delay in time, money or risk, and agree a named owner and a timebox. I go to the people involved before escalating, then use the escalation path with options rather than complaints. In parallel I look for alternatives such as a workaround or reduced scope.
questions.revision: Diagnose why it persists, make cost of delay visible, name an owner and timebox, escalate with options, and pursue alternatives in parallel.
questions.detailed:
Blockers that survive for weeks are rarely purely technical. Usually nobody owns the problem, or each team has a reasonable local priority.

## Step by step

1. **Clarify the problem.** What exactly is blocked, since when, which teams hold part of it, and what has already been tried.
2. **Find the real cause.** Ownership gap, conflicting priorities, missing access, a dependency on a vendor, or a technical disagreement.
3. **Make cost of delay visible.** Quantify: slipped milestones, engineers idle or context switching, revenue or risk exposure, compliance dates.
4. **Agree owner and timebox.** One accountable person, a decision date and a definition of resolved.
5. **Escalate with options.**
6. **Pursue alternatives in parallel.**

{{diagram:blocker}}

## Escalation path

| Level | Action |
|---|---|
| Peer to peer | Direct conversation, shared document of the facts |
| Team leads | Joint working session, timeboxed |
| Managers or sponsor | Decision request with options and cost of delay |
| Steering group | Only when priorities between teams genuinely conflict |

Escalating is not failure; doing it early and factually protects relationships.

## Alternatives

- A workaround or interim integration that removes the dependency from the critical path.
- Reduced scope, or a staged delivery that avoids the blocked part.
- Contributing the change yourselves to the other team's code, with their review.
- Accept the risk explicitly and record it in the RAID log.

## Common mistakes

- Escalating with blame rather than data and options.
- Waiting for a meeting that never happens.
- No named owner, so everyone assumes someone else is acting.
- Not recording the decision once made.
followUps: How do you estimate the cost of delay when numbers are uncertain?
What if the other team's manager disagrees about priority?
When is it better to work around than to wait?

diagrams.title: Cross-team blocker resolution
diagrams.alt: The lead diagnoses the cause, quantifies cost of delay, agrees an owner and timebox, escalates with options if needed, and in parallel explores alternatives such as workarounds or reduced scope, ending with a recorded decision.

questions.title: How do you mentor engineers who use AI assistants for development?
questions.quick: I encourage use but insist the engineer owns every line. I teach verification habits: read the generated code, run and test it, check against documentation, and explain it in review. For juniors the risk is accepting plausible code they cannot judge, so I pair on fundamentals and ask them to explain choices. To avoid skill atrophy I mix assisted and unassisted work, and review for understanding, not only output.
questions.revision: Allow AI, but the engineer owns the code: verify, test, explain it; pair juniors on fundamentals and avoid skills atrophy.
questions.detailed:
AI assistants raise productivity, but they also make it easy to ship code nobody truly understands. Mentoring shifts from "write it" to "judge it".

## Verification habits

- **Read before accepting.** Treat generated code as a suggestion from an unknown contributor.
- **Run and test.** Write or review tests first; check edge cases, error paths and security aspects.
- **Check sources.** Confirm APIs and library behaviour in official documentation, since models can invent functions.
- **Explain it.** If you cannot explain a change in review, it is not ready.
- **Disclose use** where the team agrees it is useful, so reviewers know where to look harder.

## Risks by experience level

| Level | Main risk | Mentoring response |
|---|---|---|
| Junior | Accepting plausible but wrong code; not learning fundamentals | Pair, ask for explanations, assign tasks without assistance sometimes |
| Mid-level | Over-reliance, inconsistent style | Review patterns, agree team conventions |
| Senior | Over-trusting speed, skipping design thinking | Use AI for drafts, keep design reviews |

{{diagram:mentor}}

## Avoiding skills atrophy

Alternate assisted and unassisted work, use debugging exercises where the engineer reasons first, and ask them to predict behaviour before running. Encourage using AI as a tutor ("explain this trade-off") not only as a generator.

## Team practices

Set guidance on approved tools, data that must never be pasted (secrets, customer data), and review expectations. Measure quality outcomes such as defects and review rework, not lines produced.

## Common mistakes

- Banning tools, which pushes use underground.
- Reviewing only whether the code works, not whether the author understands it.
- Letting juniors skip learning the basics.
- Pasting sensitive data into unapproved tools.
followUps: How would you review a pull request you suspect was largely generated?
What guidance would you set on sensitive data and AI tools?
How do you measure whether AI use is helping the team?

diagrams.title: Verification loop for AI-assisted code
diagrams.alt: An engineer prompts an assistant, reads the output, tests it and checks documentation, then explains it in review. Gaps in understanding lead to pairing and fundamentals practice, and the verified change is merged.

questions.title: How do you align architecture decisions with business objectives and explain them to non-technical stakeholders?
questions.quick: I begin with the business objective and the measure of success, then show how each architecture choice affects it: time to market, cost, risk or ability to change. I present two or three options with trade-offs in plain language, a recommendation and what we give up. I avoid jargon, use simple diagrams and examples, and agree decision criteria with stakeholders beforehand so the decision feels shared, not imposed.
questions.revision: Start from the business goal, present options with trade-offs in plain language, recommend, state what is given up, and agree criteria early.
questions.detailed:
Architecture is justified by the outcomes it enables. If stakeholders cannot see that link, technical quality gets cut first.

## Aligning decisions with objectives

1. **Understand the goal and metric**: revenue growth, cost reduction, regulatory deadline, customer experience.
2. **Translate into drivers**: speed to launch, flexibility, availability, security, total cost.
3. **Rank the drivers** with the sponsor, so trade-offs have an agreed basis.
4. **Choose and record** the decision in an ADR, linked to the objective.

{{diagram:align}}

## Explaining it simply

| Technical idea | Plain-language framing |
|---|---|
| Technical debt | Borrowing speed now; interest is slower changes later |
| Scalability | Ability to handle growth without rebuilding |
| High availability | How often customers can use the service |
| Vendor lock-in | Cost and effort of changing supplier later |

Use analogies sparingly, one diagram, and a concrete scenario such as "what happens during the seasonal peak".

## Presenting options

- Two or three real options, each with cost, time, risk and what it enables.
- A clear recommendation and the reasoning.
- What we are **not** getting, and the triggers that would make us revisit.
- The decision needed, from whom, by when.

## Keeping trust

Report outcomes later against the same measures. Admit when assumptions changed and adjust, so stakeholders see architecture as managed risk, not preference.

## Common mistakes

- Leading with technology names.
- Presenting one option as inevitable.
- Hiding the downsides of the favoured choice.
- Asking for approval without stating the consequence of delay.
followUps: How do you handle a stakeholder who wants a decision you disagree with?
How do you show the value of invisible work such as refactoring?
What would you include in a one-page decision summary?

diagrams.title: From business goal to decision
diagrams.alt: A business objective and success metric are translated into architecture drivers, which are ranked with the sponsor. Options are compared, a recommendation with trade-offs is presented in plain language, and the decision is recorded and later checked against the metric.

questions.title: How do you lead a team distributed across time zones?
questions.quick: I design the team to work asynchronously by default. Decisions are written down, ideally as short ADRs, so nobody waits for a meeting. I protect a small overlap window for discussion and keep it for the things that need conversation. Hand-offs use a standard note: state, next step, open risks. For releases I use a follow-the-sun readiness checklist so each region can confirm and pass on status.
questions.revision: Async by default, decisions written as ADRs, protected overlap hours, structured hand-offs and a follow-the-sun release readiness checklist.
questions.detailed:
Time zones are a constraint to design around. Teams that rely on live meetings lose a day on every question.

## Principles

- **Async first:** written proposals with a clear question and decision date; comments in the document, not scattered chat.
- **Written decisions:** short ADRs record what was decided, why and who agreed, so a region waking up has full context.
- **Overlap hours:** a protected window, rotated fairly so one region does not always take the late or early slot, used for design discussion, one-to-ones and conflict.
- **Single sources of truth:** the board, repository and runbooks, not private chats.

{{diagram:sun}}

## Hand-offs

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Current state | What is done and what is in progress |
| Next step | Exact action for the receiving region |
| Risks and blockers | Open issues and who owns them |
| Links | Pull requests, dashboards, tickets |

Use a standard template and keep it brief.

## Follow-the-sun release readiness

Each region owns a section of a shared checklist: tests and review status, environment and migration readiness, monitoring and rollback plan, support coverage. The final region confirms go or no-go with the release owner, and on-call responsibilities rotate by region so no one is permanently on call at night.

## Team health

Rotate meeting times, record sessions, respect local holidays, and invest in occasional face-to-face time or deliberate social contact. Watch for hidden isolation and uneven influence between locations.

## Common mistakes

- Making decisions in meetings that part of the team cannot attend.
- Unstructured hand-offs, so work stalls overnight.
- Always scheduling around one head office.
- No clear regional ownership at release time.
followUps: How do you reduce the delay on code review across time zones?
How would you handle an incident that spans regions?
How do you build trust between sites that rarely meet?

diagrams.title: Follow-the-sun hand-off
diagrams.alt: Work passes from one region to the next through a structured hand-off note. Regions share an overlap window for discussion, record decisions as ADRs, and each confirms release readiness before the final region gives the go or no-go.
